voters.title: Who has a vote?
voters.text: Knesset elections choose a national legislature. Citizenship, residency and location are different questions: people affected by Israeli decisions do not all have a vote in this election. Begin with the citizenship and residency distinctions.
voters.question: Does living under the effects of a government's decisions automatically give someone a Knesset vote?
options: Yes, every resident has the same national voting rights
No; eligibility depends on citizenship and other legal conditions
voters.explanation: National and municipal eligibility differ. The guide distinguishes citizens, East Jerusalem permanent residents and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza.

seats.title: Votes become 120 seats
seats.text: Voters choose a ranked electoral list in one nationwide constituency. A list needs 3.25% of valid votes to receive seats. Votes for a list below the threshold are not transferred to another list; seats are allocated among the lists that pass.
seats.question: What happens to votes cast for a list below the threshold?
options: They are transferred to its closest ally
They produce no seats for that list
seats.explanation: The threshold applies to valid votes. Passing lists share the seats; surplus-vote agreements operate between eligible passing lists, not as a rescue for a failed list.

parties.title: A party is not a bloc
parties.text: An electoral list can contain several parties. A bloc is a grouping used to describe possible alliances; it is not a single ballot choice. Read two profiles, then compare the same parties on one concrete question.
parties.question: If two lists belong to the same bloc, do they necessarily share every policy?
options: Yes; a bloc is one party with one platform
No; cooperation can coexist with policy differences
parties.explanation: Blocs describe groupings, not complete agreement. Compare recorded positions and missing evidence before describing a shared agenda.

govern.title: Who can form a government?
govern.text: The largest list does not automatically govern. It needs a governing arrangement and Knesset confidence. An absolute seat majority is 61 of 120; that planning target does not by itself establish how a confidence vote will go or whether parties will cooperate.
govern.question: Does winning the largest number of seats guarantee that a list forms the government?
options: Yes; the largest list automatically governs
No; it still needs an arrangement that can win confidence
govern.explanation: Seat arithmetic, recorded commitments and policy cooperation are separate questions. The formation guide explains the legal process; the builder helps you explore the arithmetic and constraints.

compare.title: Compare one real question
compare.text: Choose two or more lists in Compare. Find one shared recorded position and one difference. Open the evidence: what was said, when, and what remains unknown? A category count is not a forecast of governing stability.
compare.question: What can missing evidence establish?
options: That parties agree because no disagreement is recorded
compare.explanation: Silence is not agreement. Look for complete dated evidence and distinguish a shared objective from agreement on how to achieve it.
